i-vp-01.a.text: A vision system keeps classifying correctly on adversarially perturbed images.
i-vp-01.a.why: Withstanding hostile or novel input while maintaining accuracy and functionality is this side's whole job — the model never leaves its normal performance band.
i-vp-01.b.text: After degraded sensor inputs, the system returns to its specified performance limits.
i-vp-01.b.why: Bouncing back to its specified operating range after disruption — whether from harsh real-world conditions or an attack — is what this side describes; a system can be resilient without ever facing a deliberate attack.

i-vp-02.a.text: A synthetic audio clip of a public official is fabricated and spread with the deliberate goal of causing harm.
i-vp-02.a.why: Deliberate fabrication with intent to harm is the defining feature — the same false content shared by someone who believes it's real belongs on the other side.
i-vp-02.b.text: A blogger shares a deepfake video believing it's authentic, then corrects the record once the fabrication comes to light.
i-vp-02.b.why: No intent to deceive — the sharer believed the content was true — is what separates this from the deliberate-harm side of the pair.

i-vp-03.a.text: Large numbers of fake, low-fare rides are injected into a fare-prediction model's training dataset from one source.
i-vp-03.a.why: Corrupting what the model learns from, before it's ever deployed, is a training-time attack — the other side happens after the model is already live.
i-vp-03.b.text: Weeks after a spam filter goes live, an attacker salts phishing emails with invisible characters so the filter scores them as safe.
i-vp-03.b.why: Fooling a live model's outputs with crafted inputs at inference time is the other half of the pair — the model's training data was never touched.

i-vp-04.a.text: Documentation discloses what data and logic went into building the system, before anyone asks about a specific outcome.
i-vp-04.a.why: This is openness about the system's design and data — a property of the system as a whole, not of any one decision.
i-vp-04.b.text: A specific applicant asks why their case was decided the way it was, and the organization can walk through that one output in terms a person can follow.
i-vp-04.b.why: The official calibration is that a decision is explainable when its input, output and functioning are understandable to human beings — a per-decision property, distinct from transparency's system-wide openness.

i-vp-05.a.text: Confidential patient data becomes publicly accessible because a cloud storage bucket was misconfigured, with no attacker involved.
i-vp-05.a.why: Unintentional exposure through misconfiguration, not malicious activity, is what keys this side.
i-vp-05.b.text: An external actor deliberately bypasses access controls to obtain the same kind of data.
i-vp-05.b.why: Deliberate, unauthorized access by a malicious actor is the other half — the same category of harm, the opposite cause.

i-vp-06.a.text: A manufacturing defect-detector reaches near-perfect accuracy on the exact production-line photos it trained on, then misses obvious cracks in photos from a different factory line.
i-vp-06.a.why: Excellent on the training set and poor on anything new is this side's signature — the model memorized the specific photos rather than learning what a crack actually looks like.
i-vp-06.b.text: A defect-detector built with only a couple of basic image filters and no deeper layers misses cracks even in the very photos it trained on.
i-vp-06.b.why: Poor performance everywhere, including on the training data itself, signals the model never had enough complexity to capture the pattern in the first place.

i-vp-07.a.text: A radiologist stops double-checking a scan-triage tool's low-risk calls after months of accurate flags, and starts signing off on whatever it labels benign.
i-vp-07.a.why: The mechanism here is a person trusting the tool's answers so much that they stop scrutinising them — a human failure to keep checking, not a flaw baked into the data.
i-vp-07.b.text: A hiring tool trained on past hiring records rejects more candidates from minority groups, because those records already reflected who got hired before.
i-vp-07.b.why: The flaw is inherited from the training data itself, carrying forward patterns from a discriminatory past — distinct from over-trusting a tool's output once it's already deployed.

i-vp-08.a.text: A self-driving car independently decides the best route to an address the driver provides, but does nothing outside that one task.
i-vp-08.a.why: Operating within a single, limited task domain, however capable at that task, is what keeps a system on this side of the line.
i-vp-08.b.text: The same car would also need to reason, learn, and act across any task a human could, not just driving, to count as this instead.
i-vp-08.b.why: Full human cognitive ability across domains, not just excelling at one task, is what the other side requires — and it remains theoretical.

i-vp-09.a.text: A governance committee comparing two vendors asks how many billions of weight values each network ended up with once training was complete.
i-vp-09.a.why: This is the definitional line this pair tests: an internal value that training itself discovers and adjusts, which doesn't exist in final form until training is done.
i-vp-09.b.text: The same committee separately asks what learning rate and batch size the engineering team fixed before training ever began.
i-vp-09.b.why: These are choices a person makes in advance to control how training runs — inputs the team sets, not values training discovers on its own.

i-vp-10.a.text: A random forest model learns to draw the line between fraudulent and legitimate transactions.
i-vp-10.a.why: Learning the boundary between existing classes, rather than producing new examples, is this side's job.
i-vp-10.b.text: A different model, given the same transaction history, produces entirely new synthetic transaction records that never happened.
i-vp-10.b.why: Producing new content rather than classifying existing inputs is the other half of the pair.
